source: PubMed Horn of Africa 1985-1986
processing_notes: Source confirms zero cholera transmission 1987-01-01..1990-12-31. Source states: 'The prevalence of Vibrio cholerae O1 and non-O1 has been investigated in numerous Somali regions of the Horn of Africa from 1983 to 1990. From January 1983 to January 1985 and between December 1986 and December 1990, no strains of V. cholerae O1 and 226 strains (5.3%) of V. cholerae non-O1 were isolated from 4,295 diarrhea cases.'. Evidence type: Documented_Absence. Surveillance system status during absence: partial. Documented absence of epidemic Vibrio cholerae O1 in Somalia, January 1987 - December 1990, from active laboratory-based diarrhoeal surveillance across numerous Somali regions (Coppo et al., Am J Trop Med Hyg 1995;53(4):351-9, PMID 7485686). The study reports a DENOMINATOR - 4,295 diarrhoea cases cultured across Jan 1983-Jan 1985 and Dec 1986-Dec 1990 - with ZERO V. cholerae O1 isolates, which is a positive finding of absence rather than mere lack of reporting. TL set to 1987-01-01 rather than the study's 1986-12-01 so as not to conflict with the 1986 epidemic year (15 980 cases in the JHU/WHO annual baseline). CORROBORATION: (1) WER 63(20) 'Cholera in 1987' attributes part of the fall in African cases from 40 626 to 30 929 to 'the termination of the epidemic in Somalia', and Somalia appears in no WER notified-cases table for 1987, 1988, 1989 or 1990; (2) WHO's Communicable Disease Epidemiological Profile for the Horn of Africa 2007 describes the 1994 Bossaso event as 'a new laboratory-confirmed epidemic' and 'the first large-scale epidemic of cholera within Somalia'; (3) MSF's own Somalia timeline records no cholera response before 1994. CAVEATS, which is why surveillance is marked partial and confidence is downgraded below the Level 1 floor: the study covers 'numerous Somali regions', not demonstrably the whole country, and the northwest civil war from May 1988 will have degraded coverage there. CORRECTION NOTICE: the endorsed Somali Strategy for Cholera Prevention and Control 2020-2024 cites this same paper as showing 'confirmed cholera outbreaks ... from 1983 to 1990 ... the isolation of over 4,000 cases'. That is a misreading of the abstract - 4,295 is the number of diarrhoea cases CULTURED, and the finding was zero O1 isolates. Agent 1 initially recorded a presence row on the strength of the strategy's wording and removed it after checking the primary source. DOES NOT EXTEND TO 1991-1993: Coppo's surveillance ends December 1990, the state collapsed in January 1991, and there is no evidence either way for 1991-1993. Leave 1991-1993 empty.

source: WHO Weekly Epidemiological Record 61(26): Cholera in 1985
processing_notes: Source confirms zero cholera transmission 1972-01-01..1982-12-31. Source states: 'The absence of notifications from several West African countries that had experienced large outbreaks in 1984 was offset by a report of over 10 000 cases from Somalia (last affected in 1971) and considerable increases in incidence in some other countries, notably Kenya, Mali and Senegal.'. Evidence type: Documented_Absence. Surveillance system status during absence: partial. WHO's own annual global cholera review states that Somalia, reporting over 10 000 cases in 1985, was 'last affected in 1971' (French text: 'un rapport de la Somalie (ou la derniere poussee remontait a 1971)'). This is an affirmative WHO statement of absence covering 1972-1984, not merely absence from a table. Period here is capped at 1982-12-31 because 1983-01-01..1984-12-31 is covered separately and more strongly by AI row 37 (Coppo et al. laboratory denominator). CORROBORATION, four independent lines: (1) Somalia appears in no WER 'Cases of Cholera Notified to WHO' table for any year 1972-1984 - every annual WER cholera article for those years was retrieved from WHO IRIS and read individually; (2) WHO GHO's annual cholera series for Somalia has entries for 1970 and 1971 and then nothing until 1985; (3) WHO's Communicable Disease Epidemiological Profile for the Horn of Africa 2007: 'The first major outbreak of cholera in Somalia occurred in 1971 ... A second major outbreak in 1985'; (4) Coppo et al. found zero V. cholerae O1 in 1983-1984 Somali diarrhoea isolates, validating WHO's reading for the tail of this window. CAVEATS, which is why confidence is set to 0.65, well below the Level 1 floor, and surveillance to partial: (a) the evidence is substantially WHO's own non-notification record, so 'last affected in 1971' is partly a restatement of the silence rather than independent confirmation; (b) the very same WER article warns that 'there is strong reason to believe that cholera is present in a number of countries which have not notified cases in accordance with the International Health Regulations'; (c) no laboratory denominator exists for 1972-1982 comparable to Coppo's for 1983-1990. Supporting evidence that the Somalia-WHO reporting channel was live in this era: WER 52(19) of 13 May 1977 carries weekly Somali smallpox case-search returns to Geneva. Treat as probable, evidenced absence rather than certainty.
